one_liner: Schema-compiled JSON (de)serializer for AssemblyScript; on real payloads about 1-1.7x V8's JSON on 1-5 kB inputs, 3-6x on tiny ones.
what_it_does: json-as is a JSON library for AssemblyScript code compiled to WebAssembly. An asc transform (`--transform json-as`) generates a specialized `__SERIALIZE`/`__DESERIALIZE` pair for every `@json` class, so `JSON.parse<T>(str)` and `JSON.stringify(obj)` run schema-specific code instead of a generic tree walk; `JSON.Obj`/`JSON.Value`/`JSON.Arr` cover schema-less data (lazy by default since v1.5.0), and `@lazy` fields defer parsing of selected members. It mirrors the JavaScript `JSON` names but works on AssemblyScript types inside a Wasm module, so it replaces JSON handling in AS code, not `JSON.parse` in a JavaScript program.
how_it_is_fast: Codegen at build time: key bytes are packed into u64/v128 immediates and matched with direct loads, fields are dispatched by key length, and the tier-1 deserializer is an exact byte template for minified input in declaration order (with whitespace-tolerant, order-independent and scalar slow-path fallbacks). Scanning for quotes and escapes runs in one of three compile-time backends: NAIVE scalar, SWAR (64-bit words) or Wasm SIMD128 (`JSON_MODE`). Serialization writes into one reusable growable buffer (`bs`) with precomputed key bytes, floats go through the xjb64/Schubfach-based xjb-as writer, and string fields whose value is the declared default literal are emitted (or, when parsing, matched) as precomputed constants.
when_to_use: AssemblyScript services, plugins or smart contracts (WASI, edge runtimes, Wasm VMs) that exchange JSON with a fixed schema; the users listed in the README include Impart Security, Hypermode and several blockchain VMs.

Serialization-heavy paths: the v1.6.1 chart (Oct 2026, rewritten non-default benches) shows SWAR/SIMD stringify at 2,571-2,622 vs 1,580 MB/s for V8 on a 1.1 kB object (1.6x) and 4,111-4,942 vs 3,794 MB/s on 5.3 kB (1.1-1.3x).
Small messages (19-108 bytes, tokens, UUIDs, vectors) inside Wasm, where the charts show 3-6x over V8's JSON (an upper bound, because the JS harness adds an eval per operation).
Proxy, filter or forward workloads that read a few fields and re-emit the rest: lazy fields and the lazy `JSON.Obj` copy untouched source bytes straight through.
Any AssemblyScript project currently on assemblyscript-json, which the same charts place at 32-43 MB/s versus thousands of MB/s for json-as.
when_not_to_use: JavaScript applications hoping to beat `JSON.parse`: the string must cross the JS/Wasm boundary (a copy the benchmark never pays), and on 1.1 kB payloads json-as deserialize is at parity or slower even inside Wasm (761-765 vs 804 MB/s, v1.6.1 chart).
Input that is pretty-printed, reordered or carries unknown keys: it falls off the exact tier-1 template to slower tiers, and the transform's own comment puts the scalar slow path at about 5x slower.

Untrusted input in a build copied from the benchmarks: those use --noAssert, --uncheckedBehavior always and wasm-opt -tnh/-iit; strict validation is opt-in (`JSON_STRICT`), and issue #191 (failure on >1 MiB arrays containing null) is still open.
Unknown or highly dynamic documents that you read in full: the dynamic `JSON.Obj` path defers work rather than removing it, and the eager struct path needs a declared class.
Very wide schemas with `@json({ lazy: "auto" })`: the README warns stock Binaryen can crash optimizing the generated code.

integration.form: module (npm package of AssemblyScript source plus a required asc transform, `--transform json-as`)
integration.dependencies: xjb-as ^0.1.0 (float formatting); AssemblyScript compiler with the bundled transform
integration.min_toolchain: AssemblyScript asc 0.28.x (developed against ^0.28.18; issue #188 tracked a break with 0.28.16); SIMD mode needs --enable simd; mode, cache and strictness are chosen at compile time through environment variables (JSON_MODE, JSON_CACHE, JSON_STRICT, JSON_USE_FAST_PATH)
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly host (V8, Bun, Wasmtime, WAVM, wazero and WARP appear in the runtime chart); SIMD mode needs Wasm SIMD128
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the library keeps module-global state (the shared output buffer, parse traces and a last-default-source cache), so one Wasm instance should not parse re-entrantly from several threads
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same JSON.parse/JSON.stringify names, but only for AssemblyScript code with @json-decorated classes compiled through the transform; it does not replace V8's JSON in JavaScript

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the headline numbers: the v1.5.0 charts the README links (commit 0bb47d4) used benchmark classes whose declared field defaults equal the payload, and the generated code special-cases string fields that equal their default literal (constant stores on serialize; byte compare plus static-string store, no decode or allocation, on parse). The author's own default-values charts from the same run show the gap: 5.5 kB deserialize SWAR 5,734 (default) vs 1,324 MB/s (non-default) against V8's 1,295; 1.1 kB 1,321 vs 598 against 568; serialize SIMD 7,775 vs 3,161 and 3,818 vs 1,996. So the deserialize gain on 1-5 kB payloads is about 1.0-1.07x, not 2.3-4.4x.

The library-comparison bars rest on the same artifact: the 5,251-byte multilib payload is byte-identical to the compact JSON of the Repo class defaults (checked at 0bb47d4 and HEAD). Since v1.6.0 `JSON.parse<T>` first checks the whole input against that default JSON and caches the matching source pointer, returning a default-constructed object without parsing; this is how the v1.6.1 library chart reaches 12,946 MB/s vs 647 for V8, while the same run's 5.3 kB overview row is 2,122-2,251 MB/s.

The JS arm's blackbox runs `(0, eval)("%PerformMicrotaskCheckpoint();")` on every timed operation, while the AS arm does a store and load. Measured here (Node 22.22, V8 12.4, Xeon 2.1 GHz): about 180 ns per call, which took vec3 JSON.parse from 290-334 to 590-608 ns and JSON.stringify from 174-183 to 415-485 ns. On the 5 kB payload it is lost in run-to-run noise. In the 0bb47d4 run the 'Small Payload (108b)' row also compared different documents: a 108 B default-valued SessionStatusResponse in AS against a 44 B SmallJSON in JS. The Alphabet and UUIDv4 serialize rows divide by the quoted length on the AS side and the unquoted length on the JS side (+3.8% and +5.6% for AS).

Parse speed depends on input layout: the tier-1 template only fires for minified keys in declaration order. The 2026-10-05 fix PR #223 (odd-length key compare) touched only the slow path. The README's FAST_PATH_DESERIALIZE.md link returns 404.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick json-as for JSON inside AssemblyScript (it is the fast option there, far ahead of assemblyscript-json); use as-proto instead when you control both ends and can switch to protobuf, and VectorJSON when the caller is JavaScript code parsing streaming JSON, since json-as only pays off when the data already lives in Wasm memory. It pairs with as-str (same author) for string slicing around the parsed values.
verified_claims_summary: First-party d8 benchmarks (asc ^0.28.18 -O3 --noAssert --uncheckedBehavior always plus wasm-opt -O4, Ryzen 7 7800X3D, Linux 6.17). In the README-linked v1.5.0 run (V8 15.1.42, Jul 17 2026) the headline 5,734 vs 1,295 MB/s deserialize and 7,775 vs 1,062 MB/s serialize figures were measured on payloads equal to the classes' compile-time defaults; the same run's non-default variants give 1,324-1,385 vs 1,295 MB/s deserialize and 2,709-3,161 vs 1,062 MB/s serialize at 5.5 kB. The rewritten v1.6.1 run (V8 15.2.20, Oct 3 2026) gives 2,122-2,251 vs 1,883 MB/s deserialize and 4,111-4,942 vs 3,794 MB/s serialize at 5.3 kB, 761-765 vs 804 deserialize and 2,571-2,622 vs 1,580 serialize at 1.1 kB, and 3-6x on 19-52 B inputs, where V8's numbers carry the per-operation eval overhead.
status_note: Actively maintained (v1.6.1 on npm 2026-09-01, last commit 2026-10-05, 113 stars, 1 open issue, MIT) and used in production by several companies; the codec is real and fast, but the README's charts overstate the gain over V8's JSON: re-measure with non-default payloads, and record the corrected figures (and a possible retier) in a retier file.
